Main article: [Ideological leanings of United States Supreme Court justices](/wiki/Ideological_leanings_of_United_States_Supreme_Court_justices "Ideological leanings of United States Supreme Court justices")

Justices are nominated by the president in power, and receive confirmation by the Senate, historically holding many of the views of the nominating president's political party. While justices do not represent or receive official endorsements from political parties, as is accepted practice in the legislative and executive branches, advocacy groups have played a role in the selection, nomination, and confirmation process.[[153]](#cite_note-153) The Justices are often informally categorized in the media as being conservatives or liberal. Attempts to quantify the ideologies of jurists include the [Segal–Cover score](/wiki/Segal%E2%80%93Cover_score "Segal–Cover score"), [Martin–Quinn score](/wiki/Martin%E2%80%93Quinn_score "Martin–Quinn score"), and [Judicial Common Space](/wiki/Judicial_Common_Space "Judicial Common Space") score.[[154]](#cite_note-154)[[155]](#cite_note-155)

Devins and Baum argue that before 2010, the Court never had clear ideological blocs that fell perfectly along party lines. In choosing their appointments, Presidents often focused more on friendship and political connections than on ideology. Republican presidents sometimes appointed liberals, and Democratic presidents sometimes appointed conservatives. As a result, "... between 1790 and early 2010 there were only two decisions that the *Guide to the U.S. Supreme Court* designated as important and that had at least two dissenting votes in which the Justices divided along party lines, about one-half of one percent."[[156]](#cite_note-DevinsBaum-156): 316[[157]](#cite_note-DevinsBaumBook-157) Even in the turbulent 1960s and 1970s, Democratic and Republican elites tended to agree on some major issues, especially c

General Mills's corporate campus in [Golden Valley, Minnesota](/wiki/Golden_Valley,_Minnesota "Golden Valley, Minnesota")

In the 1930s, General Mills engineer, Thomas R. James, created the puffing gun, which inflated or distorted cereal pieces into puffed-up shapes. This new technology was used in 1937 to create [Kix cereal](/wiki/Kix_(cereal) "Kix (cereal)") and in 1941 to create Cheerioats (known today as Cheerios).
In 1939, General Mills engineer Helmer Anderson created the Anderson sealer. This new device allowed for bags of flour to be sealed with glue instead of just being tied with a string.
In 1956, General Mills created the tear-strip for easily opening packages.

Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932 by [King Abdulaziz](/wiki/Ibn_Saud "Ibn Saud"), who united [Hejaz](/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [Najd](/wiki/Najd "Najd"), parts of [Eastern Arabia](/wiki/Eastern_Arabia "Eastern Arabia") and [South Arabia](/wiki/South_Arabia "South Arabia") ([Asir](/wiki/Asir "Asir")) into a single state through [a series of military and political campaigns](/wiki/Unification_of_Saudi_Arabia "Unification of Saudi Arabia") beginning in 1901. The country has since been governed as an [absolute monarchy](/wiki/Absolute_monarchy "Absolute monarchy") under the [House of Saud](/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud").[[21]](#cite_note-26) In its [Basic Law](/wiki/Basic_Law_of_Saudi_Arabia "Basic Law of Saudi Arabia"), Saudi Arabia defines itself as a sovereign Arab [Islamic state](/wiki/Islamic_state "Islamic state") with [Islam as its official religion](/wiki/Islam_in_Saudi_Arabia "Islam in Saudi Arabia") and [Arabic](/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") as its official language. The ultraconservative [Wahhabi](/wiki/Wahhabism "Wahhabism") religious movement within [Sunni Islam](/wiki/Sunni_Islam "Sunni Islam") was the prevailing political and cultural force until the 2000s.[[22]](#cite_note-HT2003:_14-27)[[23]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-28) The Saudi government has attracted criticism for various policies such as its [intervention in the Yemeni Civil War](/wiki/Saudi-led_intervention_in_the_Yemeni_civil_war "Saudi-led intervention in the Yemeni civil war"), restrictions on political and civil liberties, and poor [human rights record](/wiki/Human_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia "Human rights in Saudi Arabia").[[24]](#cite_note-29)[[25]](#cite_note-30)[[26]](#cite_note-31) Since the mid-2010s, Saudi Arabia has instituted limited and gradual reforms to liberalize social, cultural, and religious life.[[27]](#cite_note-32)

* *Red Bordeaux and Red Bordeaux Supérieur*. Bordeaux winemakers may use the two regional appellations throughout the entire wine region; however, approximately half of the Bordeaux vineyard is specifically designated under Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur [AOCs](/wiki/Appellation_d%27origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e "Appellation d'origine contrôlée"). With the majority of châteaux located on the Right Bank in the Entre-Deux-Mers area, wines are typically Merlot-dominant, often blended with the other classic Bordeaux varieties. There are many small, family-run châteaux, as well as wines blended and sold by wine merchants under commercial brand names. The Bordeaux AOC wines tend to be fruity, with minimal influence of [oak](/wiki/Oak_(wine) "Oak (wine)"), and are produced in a style meant to be drunk young. Bordeaux Superieur AOC wines are produced in the same area, but must follow stricter controls, such as lower yields, and are often aged in [oak](/wiki/Oak_(wine) "Oak (wine)"). For the past 10 years, there has been strong, ongoing investment by the winemakers in both the vineyards and in the cellar, resulting in ever increasing quality. New reforms for the regional appellations were instituted in 2008 by the Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur Winemakers' Association. In 2010, 55% of all Bordeaux wines sold in the world were from Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur AOCs, with 67% sold in France and 33% exported (+9%), representing 14 bottles consumed per second.[[18]](#cite_note-CIVB_prod-18)[[19]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-19)
* *Red Côtes de Bordeaux*. Eight appellations are in the hilly outskirts of the region, and produce wines where the blend usually is dominated by Merlot. These wines tend to be intermediate between basic red Bordeaux and the more famous appellations of the left and right bank in both style and quality.
